newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai Cable Co plans $38 mln expansion.
newsitem.headline: Dubai Cable Co plans $38 mln expansion.

text.p: The Dubai Cable Co (Ducab) said on Thursday it would spend 140 million dirhams ($38 million) in the next two years expanding capacity to produce more low-voltage cables and to introduce a range of medium-voltage cables.

Ducab Managing Director Walter Bailey told a news conference the expansion was part of a previously-announced planned change in equity structure, which involves the sale of 35 percent of the company to the Abu Dhabi government.

Britain's BICC Plc will reduce its stake to 30 percent from 40, but maintain management responsibility, and the Dubai government will hold 35 percent of the firm, which is to be called the BICC-Emirates Cable Co.
Currently, Ducab is a 60-40 venture between Dubai and BICC.

Bailey said the first phase of the expansion in 1997 would involve adding more low-voltage cable capacity. In the second phase, which will run until 1998, the plant will be expanded with new medium-voltage production capacity.
Ducab manufacturing general manager Graham Cheetham said capacity would be increased to produce cable with 24,000 tonnes of copper content annually, from around 16,000 tonnes now.
"But the value will change because medium-voltage cables are worth more pro-rata in terms of copper content," he said.
Bailey said the expansion would be financed "out of our profit stream and domestic borrowing".
He said Ducab also planned to double annual sales by the year 2000 to 600 million dirhams ($163 million).

The UAE is a federation of seven emirates -- the largest and richest of which are Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Officials of both emirates who are involved in the Ducab deal would not say how much Abu Dhabi's General Industry Corp would pay for its stake.
BICC Cables operations director David Hingston said "it should not be necessary to increase capital. The company is virtually ungeared." Ducab's capital is 140 million dirhams.
Ducab chairman Abdullah Saleh said the deal was "at a very advanced stage and it is just the formalities that need to be finalised. It should be no later than the end of this year."

Asked if greater government involvement in Ducab was not contrary to regional trends towards a bigger private sector role in the economy, Ducab director Mohammad Alabbar said: "I am a believer in regionalism before privatisation. Small companies do not survive, they have to be strong first."
But Saleh said: "It is on the agenda. Privatisation is what the country is considering in future", adding that the company was "absolutely" profitable.
